title: Community safety plan approved with 2027 update
subtitle: Water permits moratorium request, Wilmot water policy deferral, council meeting hours, Charles Street lands and a hate-symbol motion.
overview: Regional Council approved the refreshed 2026-2030 Community Safety and Wellbeing Plan {{vote:m8}}. Several councillors said the plan left out issues residents raise often, such as car theft, fraud, speeding and housing. Council added a requirement that an updated plan addressing those concerns come back by June 30, 2027.

On water, council asked the Province to pause new or expanded private Permits to Take Water in areas with groundwater constraints, including the Mannheim Service Area, until the Region's Water Supply Strategy Update is done {{vote:m16}}. The decision on the 1980 Wilmot water-taking policy was deferred to a special meeting on April 8, 2026 {{vote:m12}}. Council also awarded a $20.71 million tender for Spring Valley wastewater pumping station upgrades {{vote:m5}}, and declared 15 Charles Street West in Kitchener surplus {{vote:m13}}.

Council kept the 7 p.m. start and 11 p.m. adjournment, with unanimous support needed to go later {{vote:m10}}. It also asked the federal government to name the noose as a prohibited hate symbol in Bill C-9 {{vote:m19}}. Consultants presented a council remuneration review, to be considered on April 22. Staff were asked to report on Mobility Plus service restrictions.

decisions.detail: Council approved the refreshed plan and required an updated plan addressing concerns raised at the meeting by June 30, 2027.
Council asked the Province for a temporary moratorium on new or expanded private Permits to Take Water in areas with groundwater constraints, plus more municipal notice and input on permits.
Council deferred the report on the 1980 policy to a special Council meeting on April 8, 2026, so an external consultant's information can be included.
Council accepted Baseline Constructors Inc.'s $20,710,000 tender plus taxes for upgrades at 365 Riverbend Drive, Kitchener.

decisions.item: Committee recommendations on development and facilities
decisions.detail: Council approved a tax increment grant of up to $114,580 for 161 Ottawa Street South, an updated road assumption policy, a multi-phased Charles Street Terminal plan with added reporting on public land ownership and affordable housing, and the Zero Carbon Building standard for new Regional facilities.
Council declared the former Charles Street terminal lands surplus and directed staff to prepare them for disposition and recommend a strategy.
Council chose option 2: 7 p.m. start, 11 p.m. stop, with unanimous support required to extend, to be built into the new procedural by-law.

decisions.item: Noose as hate symbol in Bill C-9
decisions.detail: Council asked the federal government to add the noose as a prohibited hate symbol in Bill C-9 and directed the Chair to send the request to federal officials and other municipalities.

debate: On the safety plan, several councillors said the four priorities matter but the plan misses concerns residents raise most: car theft, fraud against seniors, speeding, housing and youth spaces. Some also said it was brought to Council rather than committee, leaving little time for input.

Staff said the plan reflects what consultation heard, covering about 90 organisations actively and a wider network of about 150 to 170. They said it is upstream and prevention-focused, that housing and homelessness are flagged as future pillars, and that speeding did not come up in feedback. They described it as a living plan with yearly updates.

The amendment's supporters said a 15-month window would let staff address gaps without delaying submission. Council dropped the word 'preliminary' after concerns that it might conflict with provincial requirements.

A Wilmot delegate raised concerns about the Mannheim aquifer, private wells and the proposed Wilmot mega site, and asked about monitoring and accountability. A developer delegate raised concerns about development charges and delays during the water constraints.

On meeting hours, some councillors favoured an earlier start and 10 p.m. stop for better decisions and staff wellbeing. Others favoured 7 p.m. for public access and families. A few objected to requiring unanimous consent to extend.
